question: How closely can fractions approximate pi as their denominators get larger?
idea: The manuscript claims that pi has irrationality exponent exactly two. Roughly, fractions can approximate pi well, but improvements beyond the usual square-of-the-denominator scale cannot keep happening indefinitely. This is a claim about the best possible long-run approximation rate, not a new decimal expansion of pi.
why: Irrational numbers differ in how easily fractions approximate them. Locating pi precisely on this scale would answer a sharp question about its arithmetic behavior; the manuscript also claims a consequence for the Flint–Hills series.

glossary.meaning: A measure of how exceptionally well fractions can approximate a number as their denominators grow.
An irrational number cannot be written exactly as a fraction of two integers.
A rational number is a number that can be written as a fraction of two integers.

exactClaim: Proves that the irrationality exponent of π is exactly 2: for every ε > 0 and all sufficiently large denominators q, every rational $p/q$ satisfies $|\pi-p/q|\ge q^{-2-\varepsilon}$. This also proves convergence of the Flint–Hills series $\sum_{n\ge1}1/(n^3\sin^2 n)$, with angles in radians.
scope: A definition-led reading guide; the exact mathematical claim is preserved separately. This is not a proof assessment.
